Triggers.value: The same time of day the event occurred
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette: Kai had always been a man who enjoyed the early morning hours, sipping his coffee and watching the sun rise over the city before heading to work. But since that fateful day three years ago, 6:00 AM had become a dreaded time, a trigger that transported him back to the moment he was assaulted by a stranger in a deserted alley. The sound of doors opening or slamming still sent shivers down his spine, instantly bringing him back to the memory of the attacker bursting out of a doorway and pouncing on him. The event itself was etched in Kai's mind like a series of snapshots - vivid, yet disconnected moments that refused to coalesce into a coherent narrative. He remembered the feeling of being pinned against the wall, the sound of his own labored breathing, and the sensation of his phone slipping from his grasp. But there were gaps, too - moments lost in the haze of fear and confusion. When Kai recalled the event, he was consumed by an overwhelming sense of guilt, as if he had somehow brought this upon himself. In the aftermath of the assault, Kai found solace in escape. He spent hours on end playing video games, browsing social media, or watching TV shows - anything to distract him from the memories that haunted him. His partner, Rachel, would often find him glued to his phone, even when they were supposed to be spending quality time together. "I'm just taking a break," Kai would say, but deep down, he knew he was running away. As the months went by, Kai's drinking increased, too. A beer or two after work became a regular habit, and sometimes, he'd have one (or three) before bed, hoping to quiet his racing mind. Rachel expressed concern about his drinking, but Kai assured her it was under control. In reality, he felt like he needed the numbness to cope with the memories that lingered. Simple tasks, like going for a walk or running errands, became daunting challenges. Kai found himself scanning unfamiliar places, assessing potential dangers and exit routes, before deciding whether it was safe to proceed. He avoided watching TV shows or movies that depicted violence or assault, fearing they would trigger another flashback. Physical touch had also become a minefield. When Rachel surprised him with a hug or a kiss on the cheek, Kai's heart would skip a beat. He'd flinch, and she'd look at him quizzically, asking if everything was okay. "Yeah, I'm fine," he'd reply, forcing a smile. Kai couldn't shake off the feeling that the assault had somehow defined him - that it was a reflection of his character. Somebody else would have been more vigilant, more prepared, or simply more worthy of safety. He felt like he was stuck in this rut, with no hope for a future free from the shackles of trauma. It wasn't until Rachel sat him down and told him she couldn't watch him self-destruct anymore that Kai realized he needed help. She took his hand, looked into his eyes, and said, "You're not alone, Kai. We can face this together." For the first time in years, Kai felt a glimmer of hope - maybe, just maybe, he could learn to let go of the past and reclaim his life. With Rachel's support, Kai finally sought professional help, hoping to break free from the cycle of avoidance and guilt that had consumed him for so long. As he sat in the therapist's office, he knew it wouldn't be easy, but for the first time in three years, 6:00 AM felt like a new beginning rather than a harbinger of doom.
